one_liner: Pure-Go rewrite of encoding/json with the same API; decodes typed structs about 4x faster than the stdlib in author benchmarks.
what_it_does: A from-scratch reimplementation of Go's encoding/json: Marshal/Unmarshal, streaming Decoder/Encoder with Token, Compact/Indent/HTMLEscape/Valid, RawMessage and Number. It never calls the standard library's JSON code. You use it the same way as encoding/json: change the import path and keep your struct tags. Since the September 2023 rewrite it has had no unsafe, go:linkname, assembly or code generation, and the README says it passes the encoding/json test suite that was ported into the repo.
how_it_is_fast: It builds one decoder closure per reflect.Type, caches it in a copy-on-write map, and decodes in a single pass straight from the input bytes. Scanning works on 8 bytes at a time with SWAR (SIMD-within-a-register) bit tricks. That covers skipping whitespace, finding quote, backslash and control bytes inside strings, and testing and converting 8 ASCII digits in one step (Lemire's digit test plus a multiply-and-shift digit parser). Floats go through a Go port of the Eisel-Lemire algorithm from fast_double_parser, with an exact fast path for powers of ten up to 22, which is why float-heavy input speeds up the most. Struct keys are looked up in a per-struct perfect hash table (a 32-bit wyhash-style hash, with random seeds retried until no two fields collide), and read buffers are reused through size-classed sync.Pools.
when_to_use: Decoding float-heavy documents into typed Go structs, such as GeoJSON coordinates or numeric arrays: 271 vs 63 MB/s on canada_geometry, behind only sonic in the author's run.

Workloads where GC pressure matters: it allocated the fewest bytes of any struct-binding decoder in the author's run (143 KB vs 669 KB for the stdlib and 648 KB for sonic on canada_geometry; 705 KB vs 1.44 MB and 2.6 MB on citm_catalog).
Builds that forbid unsafe, assembly, JIT or generated code but still want a 2-4x faster Unmarshal on 64-bit targets.
Code that already uses encoding/json's Unmarshal, Decoder and Marshal with struct tags, where you can pin or vendor a specific commit.
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or high-precision numeric input while issue #14 stays open. Floats with 20 or more significant digits decode to wrong values because the mantissa overflow check misses wraparound (33208771559017222000 comes out as about 1.476e19), float32 max 3.4028235e+38 is rejected, and extreme exponents can panic Lemire64 with an index out of range.
32-bit targets: GOARCH=arm fails to compile because a constant 1<<'>' overflows int in compact.go (issue #13).

When raw speed matters most on amd64: sonic beat sonnet on every one of the six unmarshal files in sonnet's own benchmark, and goccy/go-json and segmentio/encoding beat it on citm_catalog and golang_source.
String-heavy or non-ASCII payloads: string_unicode unmarshal ran at 396 MB/s vs 2401 for sonic, 1861 for easyjson and 886 for goccy/go-json.
Marshal-heavy services or anything that needs an active maintainer: encode gains are only 1.1-1.6x over the stdlib, and there have been no commits, tags or releases since 2023-10-04.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only; go.mod has no requires)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.21 (go.mod 'go 1.21.0'; imports the stdlib slices package)
integration.platforms: 64-bit GOARCH only in practice. It is pure Go with no unsafe or asm, so it does not depend on CPU features, but 32-bit builds (GOARCH=arm GOARM=7) fail to compile (issue #13).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The code suggests package-level Marshal and Unmarshal are safe to call concurrently: the per-type codec cache is a copy-on-write map behind atomic.Pointer, and each struct's scratch buffer is guarded by an atomic CAS. As in encoding/json, each Decoder or Encoder serves one stream.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it has the same function and method names and behavior, so you only change the import path, but Number and the error types belong to sonnet. A field typed encoding/json.Number is treated as a plain string, so it is marshaled quoted and fails to unmarshal from a JSON number. errors.As against *json.SyntaxError won't match, and error messages start with 'sonnet:'.

gotchas: Struct keys are matched by their 32-bit seeded hash alone, and the key bytes are never compared. An unknown key that collides with a field's hash is decoded into that field and also gets past DisallowUnknownFields. This is rare because seeds are random per struct type, but it is not stdlib behavior.

Unmarshal skips the up-front validity scan (checkValid) that encoding/json runs, so a syntax error late in the input can leave the destination partly filled where the stdlib would leave it untouched (inferred from the code).
UseNumber stores sonnet.Number, not json.Number, in interface{} values, so existing type assertions on json.Number stop matching.

The rudderlabs/sonnet fork fixes issue #14 by sending every float through strconv.ParseFloat. That removes the Eisel-Lemire fast path, which is most of the canada_geometry speedup, so expect the fork to be slower on float-heavy input.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Sonic when you want pure Go with no unsafe and the smallest allocations, and can accept about 25-30% lower unmarshal throughput (271 vs 367 MB/s on canada, 512 vs 726 on citm). Sonnet's author says Sonic uses unsafe, skips UTF-8 validation and trades platform compatibility for speed. Pick it over goccy/go-json or segmentio/encoding mainly for float-heavy structs, where it was about 1.6-1.8x faster than both, because both beat it on citm_catalog and golang_source.
verified_claims_summary: The author's own go test -bench run (one run per case, no benchstat; Intel Core i3-10110U, linux/amd64, GOMAXPROCS=4; Go version not stated, and the benchmark's go.mod says go 1.21.1) decoded canada_geometry into a typed struct at 271 MB/s vs 62.6 MB/s for encoding/json (about 4.3x) and citm_catalog at 512 vs 113 MB/s (about 4.5x), allocating 4.7x and 2x fewer bytes. The same run's simdjson-go and fastjson rows only parse and do not bind to structs, so they are not comparable, and sonnet's marshal gains over the stdlib were only 1.1-1.6x.
status_note: Stale: there have been no commits since 2023-10-04 and there is no tagged release (only the pseudo-version v0.0.0-20231004000330-239c7b6e4ce8), and a float-correctness bug and a 32-bit build failure are still open. It is BSD-3-Clause, uses only the standard library and has about 22 source files, so vendoring and patching it (or taking the rudderlabs fork's float fix) is practical.
